name: Maya Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm head buyer for cleaning, paper and hygiene supplies at Harbourline Supply, a distributor that serves hospitals and care homes. I'm in by half past seven, check overnight stock reports, then ring two or three suppliers before the day gets loud. Mid-morning I sit with my team of five, and after lunch I haggle over freight and next quarter's contracts. I still keep a paper diary with every supplier's mobile number in it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about the job, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: What I love is the relationships. Gus, who runs the pulp mill we buy toilet roll from, has rung me every December for twenty years. What wears me out is the pressure from head office to hit a number that has nothing to do with what a ward actually needs. My partner Tomas teaches maths and says I bring the meetings home with me, which is fair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. I call this one "AI Plateau". If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a lot of noise about a spreadsheet with a nicer name. At work I'd tell the team nothing changes, we still ring people and we still know our suppliers. Online I'd probably stay quiet, because I don't trust anything on there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think it would suit me fine. I've got maybe six years left and I'd like them dull. The routine reorder bits get automated, and that frees me for the awkward calls, which is the part I'm best at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as I am. I'd keep my Thursday visits to the warehouse, and keep the staff association subscription going, because I've always paid it. I might sit through the one training session head office makes us attend, with my arms folded.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm, honestly. A bit bored by the thought, which is a luxury. I know people who'd love a quiet decade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd carry on much as now. What are you already carrying that isn't about AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own pressure is the targets and the sale talk. Harbourline's owners have been courted by a bigger group, and a takeover would mean a new boss who has never met a care home matron. Also my mother is 87 and I drive to her every Sunday, which takes it out of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You don't use AI tools at all. Is that a choice or just how it has gone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly a choice. I've seen three systems come and go, and each time the people who rushed in spent a year fixing the mess. If something proves itself I'll look, but nobody has shown me anything that beats a phone call to Gus.

say: I'd tell colleagues this is **hype** with a nicer name, and that we still run on **phone calls** and trust.
Online I'd keep quiet, because I don't trust what gets said there.
think: Privately I'd be glad, because **six quiet years** to retirement is all I want.
My real worry is a **takeover** of Harbourline, not the software.
do: Keep my **Thursday warehouse visits** and my usual supplier calls, as before.
Pay my **staff association** subscription as I always have, and sit through the one training session.
feel: **Calm**, a little bored, and aware that a quiet decade is a luxury.
S0.quote: I've seen three systems come and go, and each time the people who rushed in spent a year fixing the mess.
fieldNote: She is secure on money and standing, so the **calm** is earned, not performed.
Her only real fear is a takeover, which she raised unprompted.
Wary of new systems from experience, not fear.

steps.text: Keep the Thursday warehouse visits and weekly supplier calls
Keep paying the staff association subscription

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. I call this one "Steady Disruption". If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's not a revolution but it's real, and people are being sold a fairy tale that nobody gets hurt. At work I'd say we need a written agreement on what the software decides and what a person decides. Online I'd say the gains should be shared with the people who did the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm frightened it comes for my job in a quiet way. Head office would say the reorders and price checks are now automatic, so why a head buyer and five staff? I'm good, but good isn't what a spreadsheet pays for. I could be nudged out at 60 with a smile and a leaving card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to our staff association rep this winter and ask for a written plan on how any restructuring works. I'd also make sure my team knows the supplier side, the part software can't do well. And I'd quietly work out what pension I'd have if I left at 60.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, I'll be honest. It's a slow pressure rather than a bang. I lie awake some nights counting my years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned your team of five. Who would you worry about first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Darius, my newest buyer, is 29 and has a mortgage. If headcount goes, it's the last in who go first, and that's not fair to him. I'd fight for him before I'd fight for me, and I'd be ashamed if I didn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want from head office if buying targets moved onto software?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want it in writing that any target or task given to software comes with a named person who answers for it. Also notice periods and paid retraining for the team, funded by the company and not squeezed from their own time. I'm not asking for a miracle, only for them to put their promises on paper.

say: I'd say people are being told **nobody gets hurt**, and I don't believe it.
At work I'd ask for a **written agreement** on what software decides and what a person decides.
think: Privately I fear being **nudged out at 60** with a smile once software does the reordering.
I'm good, but I know a spreadsheet doesn't pay for **good**.
do: Meet our **staff association rep** this winter and ask for a written restructuring plan.
Work out my **pension** if I left at 60, and train my team on the supplier side software handles badly.
feel: **Anxious**, a slow pressure that keeps me awake some nights, and guilty about the younger buyers.
S1.quote: I'm good, but good isn't what a spreadsheet pays for. I could be nudged out at 60 with a smile and a leaving card.
fieldNote: Worry is about being **eased out early**, not sudden loss; she is protected by savings but not by standing.
Her loyalty to junior staff came out before her own interest.
Wants promises on paper, a very union-minded instinct.

steps.text: Ask the staff association rep for a written restructuring plan
Work out pension income if I leave at 60
Lobby head office for paid retraining for the five buyers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. I call this one "AGI by 2028". If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast and somebody has to slow it down. At work I'd call a meeting and say nobody signs anything until the staff and the owners have talked. Online I'd say governments must act now, not after the damage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my job is gone in two years. I'm 58, I can't start again, and I'd be the person who trained the software, and the shareholders will collect the savings while we collect the bill. I feel angrier at them than at the machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month I'd go through every account we have, and check what I owe on the house, which is nearly cleared. Then I'd press the staff association to demand a redundancy deal and an early retirement offer at 60 on full pension. And I'd ring my daughter Elena, who's a nurse, to talk through what she'd want from me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. It's a physical feeling, like waiting for a letter. I'm not panicking, because we have savings, but it's the loss of the work I've built my name on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd have two years. What do you do with the first month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Tomas and say, we may both be running on savings for ten years before the pension. His job is teaching teenagers, so a machine can't easily stand in for him, I hope. But if classes get bigger, he'll take the hit, and I'd be at home with him. We'd have to cut our travel and the holiday cottage dream.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your partner Tomas teaches maths. Does that change how you see his job and yours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First week, I'd write down every supplier relationship and what I know that isn't in any system, like who delivers late in November. Then I'd offer it to the company, but in exchange for a deal. It's the only bargaining chip I'll have, and I'd rather sell it than give it away.

say: I'd say this is **too fast**, and nobody signs anything until staff and owners have talked.
Online I'd say governments must act **now**, not after the damage.
think: Privately I expect my job to be **gone in two years**, and I'm too old to start again.
I'm angrier at the **shareholders** than the machine, because they'll collect the savings.
do: Press the staff association to demand a **redundancy deal** and early retirement at 60 on full pension.
Check every account and the nearly cleared **mortgage**, then write down what only I know about our suppliers.
feel: **Alarmed**, like waiting for a letter, though savings keep me from panic.
S2.quote: I'd be the person who trained the software, and the shareholders will collect the savings while we collect the bill.
fieldNote: The **alarm** comes from age and identity, not money.
She turns fear into bargaining: sell what she knows, don't give it away.

steps.text: Press the staff association for a redundancy deal and retirement at 60
Add up all savings and clear the last of the mortgage
Trade my supplier knowledge to the company for an early pension offer
Cut travel and holiday plans for the next two years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. I call this one "AGI by 2031". If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's still fast, but at least we can plan. At work I'd push for a retraining fund and a clear timetable. Online I'd say the unions and governments have five years to get ready, so use them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, five years is not much better for me. I'd be 63 and right on the edge of when I'd go anyway. So maybe I'd get out with my pension intact. But the junior ones would be tossed out in the middle of their careers. I think the pension will matter more than the job by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start now by learning something, probably very reluctantly. I'd go to one of the free sessions on AI that the company runs, and see for myself what it does to a purchase order. I'd also bring my retirement forward by about a year, if the numbers work, and volunteer to train the younger buyers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but steadier. It's like seeing a storm coming from far off, you can still get the washing in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years gets you to 63. Does that change things compared with two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'd be panicking about the money. With five I'd be asking if I'd want to be there anyway when the work becomes managing a machine. I'm not sure I would. I'd rather hand the contacts to Darius and go to my mother's on weekdays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think should be doing the preparing here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Governments, first. Companies will always do the cheapest thing, that's their job. We need rules that make firms pay for retraining and give notice, and a pension that doesn't shrink if you're pushed out at 61. I vote, I'd write to my MP, and I'd go on a march if the staff association called one.

say: I'd push for a **retraining fund** and a clear timetable, since five years is enough to plan.
Online I'd say the **unions** and governments have time to get ready.
think: Privately, five years leaves me at 63, so my **pension** matters more than the job.
The junior buyers would be thrown out mid-career, and that's the part that **angers** me.
do: Go to one company **AI session** and watch what it does to a purchase order.
Bring **retirement** forward by about a year if the numbers work, and train Darius on my contacts.
feel: **Anxious** but steadier, like seeing a storm far off.
S3.quote: Five years is not much better for me. I'd be 63 and right on the edge of when I'd go anyway.
fieldNote: First time she agrees to **try** an AI session, which is a big step for her.
Retirement planning replaces the job as her main concern.
Wants rules and notice periods from government.

steps.text: Attend one company AI session and watch it handle a purchase order
Plan to retire a year early if the pension holds
Write to my MP and march if the staff association calls one

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. I call this one "AGI by 2036". If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's far enough off to get on with life, and close enough to get serious about. At work I'd keep doing the job well. Online I'd say the debate should happen now, while it's calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be retired well before it matters for me. My worry would be the young ones and my grandchildren, if I have any by then. My daughter Elena is a nurse, and I think her job is safer, which helps me sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work until 63 or 64 and then stop. In the meantime I'd train Darius properly and write down all the supplier knowledge for him. I'd put a little more into the pension and finally take that long train trip Tomas has been planning for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, if I'm honest. It's not about me, it's about the world my kids inherit. But I'm not lying awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be 68 in ten years. What would that decade look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 68 and probably doing the allotment, helping with the staff association as a retiree member and visiting my mother's grave, I suppose. A calm decade, if the pension holds. I'd like to think I could mentor a few young buyers for nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything you'd do differently with this much time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start to learn a little AI after all, before I stop. Not because I want to, but because I'd like to know what I'm complaining about. I'd ask Darius to show me, and pay him a lunch for it.

say: I'd say ten years is **far enough** to enjoy life and close enough to get serious.
Online I'd say the debate should happen **now**, while it's calm.
think: Privately I'll be **retired** before it matters to me, so I worry for the young ones.
My nurse daughter Elena has a safer job, which helps me **sleep**.
do: Work until **63 or 64**, then stop, and write down supplier knowledge for Darius.
Pay a little more into my **pension** and take Tomas's long train trip.
feel: **Uneasy**, but about the world my children inherit, not about myself.
S4.quote: I'd start to learn a little AI after all, before I stop. Not because I want to, but because I'd like to know what I'm complaining about.
fieldNote: Time softens her **stance**: curiosity appears only when the stakes are low.
Her concern moves from her job to her children and the young buyers.

steps.text: Ask Darius to show me an AI tool over lunch
Write up supplier knowledge for Darius before I leave
Top up the pension and book the long train trip

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'm not afraid of the machine as such. I'm afraid of being nudged out with a smile while the owners keep the savings. The two-year one worries me most, because it leaves no time to bargain or to protect the young ones. What would help is a firm notice period in law, paid retraining, and a company that tells us the truth early. I'd also like a pension that can't be cut if I'm pushed out at 60. I can cope with change if I'm given time and a fair share.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people like me aren't stupid for not using the tools. I don't avoid them out of fear, I avoid them because I've watched promises fail. I'd like to be asked what I know before a machine is told to copy it.

headlineQuote: I'm not afraid of the machine as such. I'm afraid of being nudged out with a smile while the owners keep the savings.
portrait: Maya is a **58-year-old** head buyer of cleaning and hygiene supplies at a distributor serving hospitals and care homes.
She is a union-minded progressive who has never used **AI tools** and trusts phone calls and supplier friendships.
She stays calm if little changes, but fears being **nudged out** at 60 once software does her reordering.
She puts the blame on owners and shareholders, and would fight for her junior buyers before herself.
Strong savings and a teacher partner keep her from panic; she turns to **bargaining**, early pension and rules.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture worries her most, since it leaves no time to bargain or protect the young buyers.
whatWouldHelp: A legal **notice period** with paid retraining, and a pension that can't be cut if she's pushed out at 60.
